q-95080.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14248773/assets/7e5b5001794ecdf2c9b9e9102f334a63d2c59bc6f7511c2eb7fa358fc94cb0c5.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $s,$ where $x=x(s)$ and $y=y(s),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}={e}^{x+2y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2{e}^{x+2y}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & ={e}^{{s}^{2}+2s}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =2{e}^{{s}^{2}+2s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}=2s,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s} \\  & ={e}^{{s}^{2}+2s}\cdot 2s+2{e}^{{s}^{2}+2s}\cdot 1 \\  & =2s{e}^{{s}^{2}+2s}+2{e}^{{s}^{2}+2s} \\  & =2(s+1){e}^{{s}^{2}+2s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

If f(x,y)=ex+2y,x=s2, and y=s, compute dfds.

a
2ses2+2s
b
2(s+2)es2+2s
c
2(s+1)es2+2s
d
s(s+2)es2+2s
e
s2es2+2s
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) with one independent variable s, where x=x(s) and y=y(s), can be expressed as follows:

dfds=∂f∂x⋅dxds+∂f∂y⋅dyds

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y:

∂f∂x=ex+2y,∂f∂y=2ex+2y

Writing the above results in terms of s, we get

∂f∂x=es2+2s,∂f∂y=2es2+2s.

Next, we take the derivatives of x and y with respect to s, and we get

dxds=2s,dyds=1.

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

dfds=∂f∂x⋅dxds+∂f∂y⋅dyds=es2+2s⋅2s+2es2+2s⋅1=2ses2+2s+2es2+2s=2(s+1)es2+2s.

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-\frac{1}{(x+y)^{2}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-\frac{1}{(x+y)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-\frac{1}{(x+{e}^{-x})^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-{e}^{-x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{1}{(x+{e}^{-x})^{2}}-\frac{1}{(x+{e}^{-x})^{2}}\cdot (-{e}^{-x}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{(x+{e}^{-x})^{2}}+\frac{{e}^{-x}}{(x+{e}^{-x})^{2}} \\  & =\frac{-1+{e}^{-x}}{(x+{e}^{-x})^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

a
−1+e−x(x+e−x)2

dfdx=∂f∂x+∂f∂y⋅dydx

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y:

∂f∂x=−1(x+y)2,∂f∂y=−1(x+y)2

Writing the above results in terms of x, we get

∂f∂x=∂f∂y=−1(x+e−x)2.

Next, we take the derivative y with respect to x, and we get

dydx=−e−x.

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

dfdx=−1(x+e−x)2−1(x+e−x)2⋅(−e−x)=−1(x+e−x)2+e−x(x+e−x)2=−1+e−x(x+e−x)2.

q-95114.worked_solution:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{x}^{6}}} \\  & =\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}(1+{x}^{4})}} \\  & =\frac{x}{x\sqrt{1+{x}^{4}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+{x}^{4}}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{{x}^{3}}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{x}^{6}}} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}(1+{x}^{4})}} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}}{x\sqrt{1+{x}^{4}}} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{\sqrt{1+{x}^{4}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =3{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+{x}^{4}}}+\frac{{x}^{2}}{\sqrt{1+{x}^{4}}}\cdot 3{x}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+{x}^{4}}}+\frac{3{x}^{4}}{\sqrt{1+{x}^{4}}} \\  & =\frac{1+3{x}^{4}}{\sqrt{1+{x}^{4}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14248773/assets/f01b253f560405a8c0f4be8f8797c652fb0ddf774f4db110b8822313b8ac50f3.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $t,$ where $x=x(t)$ and $y=y(t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡({t}^{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(t), \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡({t}^{2})\operatorname{sin}⁡(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=2t,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡({t}^{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\cdot 2t+(-\operatorname{sin}⁡({t}^{2})\operatorname{sin}⁡(t))\cdot 1 \\  & =2t\operatorname{cos}⁡({t}^{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡({t}^{2})\operatorname{sin}⁡(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{2xy}{{x}^{2}+1},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{2x({x}^{2}+1)}{{x}^{2}+1}=2x, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =2x+\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)\cdot 2x \\  & =2x(1+\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

If f(x,y)=yln⁡(x2+1) and y=x2+1, compute dfdx.

a
2xln⁡(x2+1)
b
2x(1+ln⁡(x2+1))
c
2xln⁡(x2+1)
d
2x(x2+1)ln⁡(x2+1)
e
(x2+1)ln⁡(x2+1)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) in the case where y=y(x) can be expressed as follows:

dfdx=∂f∂x+∂f∂y⋅dydx

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y:

∂f∂x=2xyx2+1,∂f∂y=ln⁡(x2+1)

Writing the above results in terms of x, we get

∂f∂x=2x(x2+1)x2+1=2x,∂f∂y=ln⁡(x2+1).

Next, we take the derivative y with respect to x, and we get

dydx=2x.

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

dfdx=2x+ln⁡(x2+1)⋅2x=2x(1+ln⁡(x2+1)).
